topic: The Pi Collision Puzzle: Why Counting Bounces Reveals the Universe's Most Famous Constant
target_audience: High school students and undergraduate physics/math enthusiasts

sections.title: The Setup: A Curious Experiment
lecture_lines: Imagine two blocks sliding on a frictionless floor.
A wall sits on the far left side.
A large block collides with a stationary small block.
We count every collision between blocks and the wall.
Watch as the collision count reveals digits of Pi.
animations: Create a white wall (#FFFFFF) on the far left and a horizontal floor line (#FFFFFF).
Draw a small block (#00FF00) labeled 'm' and a large block (#0000FF) labeled 'M' stationary on the floor.
Animate the large block 'M' (#0000FF) sliding from the right edge toward the small block (#00FF00).
Create a yellow collision counter (#FFFF00) at the top of the screen starting at zero.
Flash the yellow counter (#FFFF00) with numbers 3, 31, 314 as collisions occur.

sections.title: Prerequisite Knowledge: The Laws of the Game
lecture_lines: Energy conservation keeps the system's total speed restricted.
Momentum conservation governs how velocity transfers between blocks.
These physical laws define the rules of every hit.
animations: Display 'Energy Conservation' in green (#00FF00) and 'Momentum Conservation' in blue (#0000FF) at the top of the screen.
Show a pulsing green battery icon (#00FF00) in the center to represent kinetic energy.
Draw blue directional arrows (#0000FF) between the blocks during a collision to show momentum transfer.

sections.title: Mapping to Phase Space: The Velocity Vector
lecture_lines: We plot velocities on a two-dimensional graph.
Each point represents the current state of both blocks.
Collisions cause this state point to jump around.
animations: Create a 2D coordinate system with axes v1 (blue #0000FF) and v2 (green #00FF00), plus a yellow state point (#FFFF00).
Add a label 'System State' next to the yellow point (#FFFF00) to show it represents both blocks.
Animate the yellow point (#FFFF00) jumping between positions, leaving a thin white trail (#FFFFFF) behind.

sections.title: The Geometry of Energy: Stretching the Circle
lecture_lines: Energy conservation forms an elliptical path on our graph.
We rescale the axes to simplify the geometry.
The ellipse transforms into a perfect, uniform circle.
The system's state now moves along this circular boundary.
Geometry reveals hidden patterns in the block dynamics.
animations: Draw a green ellipse (#00FF00) centered at the origin of the velocity graph.
Display the scaling factors sqrt(M) and sqrt(m) in white (#FFFFFF) next to the axes.
Animate the green ellipse (#00FF00) stretching vertically until it becomes a perfect cyan circle (#00FFFF).
Add a bright cyan glow (#00FFFF) to the perimeter of the circle to highlight the state boundary.
Fade in a yellow Pi symbol (#FFFF00) at the center of the cyan circle.

sections.title: The Secret Angle: Why Pi?
lecture_lines: Each collision rotates the state by a constant angle.
This angle depends on the ratio of block masses.
We count how many jumps fit within the circle.
Total collisions equal the total arc divided by angle.
Half the circle represents Pi radians of total rotation.
animations: Show the yellow state point (#FFFF00) performing discrete jumps along the arc of the cyan circle (#00FFFF).
Draw two magenta radial lines (#FF00FF) from the center to consecutive points to highlight the angle 'theta'.
Animate the magenta angle 'theta' (#FF00FF) shrinking as the mass M is visually increased.
Highlight the top half-arc of the circle in white (#FFFFFF) to represent the total rotation of Pi radians.
Display the calculation 'Hits = Pi / Theta' in white (#FFFFFF) as the point completes its traversal.

sections.title: Conclusion: The Final Tally
lecture_lines: Larger mass ratios create smaller, more precise angles.
The collision count perfectly matches the digits of Pi.
A surprising link between simple physics and mathematical constants.
animations: Show the block simulation with a yellow collision counter (#FFFF00) displaying the value '3141'.
Display a white table (#FFFFFF) mapping mass ratios (1, 100, 10000) to collision counts (3, 31, 314).
Fade out all elements except the yellow counter, which transforms into the mathematical symbol for Pi (#FFFF00).
